title: Greedy and backtracking in Python (list copies, itertools, recursion limit)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Jump game, subsets, combination sum and word search with list backtracking, snapshots with cur[:], mutable default arguments and itertools pitfalls.
source: Python docs (itertools, list, defaults, sys.setrecursionlimit); CLRS ch. 16; LeetCode Jump Game, Subsets, Combination Sum, Word Search

questions.prompt: Write a Python function can_jump(nums). You start at index 0 and nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. Return True if the last index is reachable, in O(n) time using a greedy farthest-reach variable.
questions.explanation: Greedy works because reachable indices form a prefix: if you can reach index r, you can reach everything before it. A backwards "goal post" loop is an equally valid O(n) solution. For [2,3,1,1,4] the result is True and for [3,2,1,0,4] it is False.

checks.label: tracks the farthest reachable index with max
uses i + nums[i] as the candidate reach
returns False when the current index is beyond the reach

questions.prompt: Write a Python function subsets(nums) that returns all subsets (the power set) of a list of distinct integers using backtracking with a nested helper.
questions.explanation: The copy cur[:] is essential: appending cur itself would leave every entry pointing at the same, finally empty list. There are 2^n results, each copied in O(n). An include/exclude recursion or a bitmask loop are also valid.

checks.label: adds a copy of the current path to the result
chooses with append and un-chooses with pop (backtrack)

questions.prompt: Write a Python function combination_sum(cands, target) that returns all unique combinations of the positive integers in cands that sum to target, where each number may be reused. Sort first and prune once a candidate exceeds the remaining target.
questions.explanation: Starting each loop at start (not 0) prevents [2,3] and [3,2] both appearing. Passing i (not i + 1) is what allows reuse. The break is valid only because the list is sorted. Immutable alternatives (cur + [x]) avoid the pop.

checks.label: sorts the candidates to enable pruning
prunes with break (or return) when a candidate is too big
recurses on the same index so numbers can be reused
appends a copy of the path and pops after recursing

questions.prompt: Write a Python function exist(board, word) that returns True if word can be traced in a grid of characters through horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell at most once per path.
questions.explanation: Restoring the cell after the recursive calls is the backtracking step. Worst case O(R C 4^L) for a word of length L (each step has at most 3 fresh directions in practice). A visited set that you add to and remove from is equally valid.

checks.label: compares the cell with the next letter of the word
marks the cell as used while exploring
returns True on a full match

questions.prompt: How many tuples does len(list(itertools.combinations(range(6), 3))) return?
questions.explanation: These are the 3-element subsets of 6 items: C(6, 3) = 20. itertools.combinations yields them in lexicographic order without repeats.

questions.prompt: How many tuples does len(list(itertools.permutations('AABC'))) return?
questions.explanation: permutations treats elements as distinct by position, not by value, so the two A's produce duplicates: 4! = 24 tuples, of which only 12 are distinct. Wrap in set(...) or sort and skip equal neighbours to deduplicate.

questions.prompt: In Python backtracking, which statement correctly records the current path cur in the results list res?
questions.explanation: list(cur) and cur.copy() also work. Immutable tuples or new lists (cur + [x]) avoid both the copy and the pop.

options.why: Correct: the slice makes a separate copy that later pops cannot change.
This stores a reference, and the path keeps changing as the recursion continues.
This stores one removed element and damages the path being built.
This flattens the path into the results instead of storing it as a subset.

questions.prompt: In the Python subsets backtracking, why does the loop use range(start, len(nums)) instead of range(len(nums))?
questions.explanation: Starting at 0 would generate permutations of subsets and duplicates. With start, the recursion tree has exactly 2^n nodes.

options.text: So each subset is built once, in index order.
options.why: Correct: moving only forward yields every combination exactly once.

options.text: Because range(len(nums)) would raise an IndexError on the last item.
options.why: range(len(nums)) yields valid indices only; nothing would raise.

options.text: To keep the list sorted, since Python lists lose their order after a pop.
options.why: pop leaves the order of the remaining items unchanged.

options.text: Because Python limits recursion to one call per loop index.
options.why: Python imposes no such limit; the depth limit is a separate matter.

questions.prompt: True or false: writing def go(path=[]) as a recursive helper is risky, because the same default list is shared by every call that omits the argument.
questions.explanation: Use path=None and create a fresh list inside, or pass the list explicitly. This is one of the most common Python backtracking bugs.

options.why: Correct: the default is evaluated once at definition time, so all calls reuse one list.
The default list is created once, so the statement is true and mutations leak between calls.

questions.prompt: A backtracking function appends cur to the results and later calls cur.pop().
questions.explanation: Snapshot with cur[:], list(cur) or cur.copy() before storing.
questions.assertion: Executing res.append(cur) instead of res.append(cur[:]) leaves every stored subset equal to the final state of cur.
questions.reason: cur is one mutable list that the recursion keeps modifying.

whys.a: Right: all entries are references to the same list, which ends up empty, and R is the reason.
whys.b: R is the explanation, not a side fact.

questions.explanation: On unsorted input a too-large candidate must be skipped with continue, not break.
questions.assertion: Sorting the candidates lets the loop break as soon as one exceeds the remaining target.
questions.reason: sorted returns a new list and leaves the original list unchanged.

whys.a: Returning a new list is not why sorting enables the break; the ascending order is.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but the break works because larger candidates follow, not because sorted copies the list.

questions.prompt: Backtracking over subsets of n items recurses n levels deep.
questions.explanation: Depth n is small for subsets, but a DFS over 10^5 nodes would hit the limit; use an explicit stack there.
questions.assertion: The recursion depth of subset backtracking is only n.
questions.reason: Python's default recursion limit is about one million frames.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but the default limit is about 1000 frames, so R is false.

questions.explanation: Use set(permutations(...)), or sort and skip equal neighbours in your own backtracking.
questions.assertion: The call returns exactly 3 distinct permutations.
questions.reason: itertools.permutations treats elements as unique by position, not by value.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true and is why A is false; the call returns 6 tuples, of which 3 are distinct.

questions.prompt: Match each backtracking need with the Python idiom that serves it.
questions.explanation: Each idiom serves one step of choose, explore, un-choose. clear() would wipe the whole path rather than the last choice.

left.text: Store a snapshot of the current path
Group equal values so duplicates can be skipped
Enumerate k-element subsets without writing recursion
Mark a grid cell as visited in place

questions.prompt: Complete the Python bitmask enumeration of subsets.
questions.explanation: The range covers 2^n masks. Shifting right by j then & 1 isolates bit j; a non-zero (truthy) result means the item is included.
questions.text: Loop mask over range(1 << {1}); item j belongs to the subset when (mask >> j) & {2} is {3}.
